summary: For ages 12–14: teach extinction as a RACE OF RATES — the speed of environmental change versus the speed at which a population can adapt by natural selection — rather than a species being 'weak' or 'failing to try'. Learners manipulate both rates for the same population, see selection track slow change but lose the race under fast change, explore vulnerability factors (generation time, genetic variation, specialism), distinguish background from mass extinction, and connect the reasoning to human-driven present-day losses. A role-play argument and a case gallery deepen and extend the core model. The simulation is one representation among several, not a uniquely necessary or proven-superior medium.
misconceptions: Thinking extinct species were simply 'weak', 'lazy' or 'failed to try', rather than unable to adapt fast enough to change.
Believing a species can adapt on demand within a generation or two when the environment changes suddenly.
Assuming extinction is always caused by a single dramatic event (asteroid), missing gradual and multi-driver causes.
Confusing background extinction with mass extinction, or thinking extinction is entirely abnormal rather than a constant low-level process.
Thinking humans are separate from these processes, rather than the primary driver of the current accelerated extinction rate.
Believing that because life recovered after past mass extinctions, current biodiversity loss is nothing to worry about — ignoring the million-year recovery timescales.

activities.title: The survival race: dial the rate of change against the rate of adaptation
steps: Start a scenario where a population with heritable variation faces a changing environment (e.g. gradual warming, or a newly arrived predator) and set the environmental change to a slow rate.
Watch two linked displays at once: the trait distribution shifting generation by generation via selection, and the total population size over time.
Observe that under slow change, selection tracks the environment, the trait distribution slides to match, and the population holds steady — the species survives.

Push the rate-of-change slider higher and watch selection fall behind: the trait distribution cannot shift fast enough, numbers plunge, and the population reaches EXTINCT — the very same species that survived slow change.

Handicap the species using vulnerability levers — long generation time, little genetic variation, high specialism — and compare, in the model, how a slow-breeding, low-variation specialist dies out where a fast-breeding, variable generalist scrapes through at the same rate of change.
Switch into a 'background vs mass' comparison: a steady low trickle of extinctions versus a sudden catastrophic pulse, and note the different pattern each produces.
Press a 'switch to today's rate' option to see how current extinction rates, driven largely by human-caused change, compare with the background extinction rate.
activities.insight: Extinction can happen when environmental change outpaces the generations-long, variation-dependent process of adaptation — a mismatch of rates, not a species simply being weak or failing. Which species survive rapid change depends partly on generation time, available heritable variation, and degree of specialism (as well as factors such as population size and ability to disperse).

activities.title: Argue the case: interview a conservation biologist or palaeontologist
steps: Take part in a role-play interview with a palaeontologist (about the dodo or woolly mammoth) or a conservation biologist (about a species on the brink today).
Respond to the challenge 'Why couldn't it just adapt?' by explaining the rate mismatch and the species' specific vulnerability factors.

Respond to 'Why are today's extinction rates different from normal?' by distinguishing background from mass extinction and naming human drivers (habitat loss, overexploitation, pollution, climate change).
Marshal observations from the survival-race activity into a short, evidence-based argument about whether a named species can keep pace with current change.
activities.insight: The argue-from-evidence objective asks learners to turn the rate-race model into a defended explanation of why a given species could not keep pace and why current rates exceed the background rate.

activities.title: Hall of extinction: case gallery and geological timeline
steps: Explore a gallery of extinct and endangered species — dodo, woolly mammoth, thylacine, plus contemporary cases such as amphibians or coral — revealing for each one its vulnerability factors and the specific change that outpaced it.
Place each case on a geological timeline that marks the five past mass extinctions and the current pulse.
For each species, state in your own words what outpaced its ability to adapt and why.
Sort species into higher or lower vulnerability and justify each choice using generation time, genetic variation, and specialism.
activities.insight: The same rate-mismatch logic explains extinctions across deep time and the present; vulnerability factors help predict which species survive rapid change. Background extinction is a steady ongoing process, distinct from rare catastrophic mass-extinction pulses.

activities.title: Check and apply: diagnostic on 'animals will just evolve in time'
steps: Judge the claim: 'As the climate warms very fast, don't worry — animals will just evolve quickly to cope, so they won't go extinct.' Decide whether the reasoning is sound and explain when a species CAN adapt in time and when it can't.
Answer the follow-up: the same warming happens slowly over 50,000 years instead of 100 years — does your answer change, and why?
Answer: there are 30 individuals of a species left, all in one zoo — is that species safe? Why or why not?
Explain how the current rate of extinction differs from the background rate and what is driving the difference.
Match each historical case to what outpaced it, and distinguish an example of background extinction from a mass extinction.
activities.insight: A learner who grasps the rate argument rejects 'just evolve in time', ties survival to change being slower than the generational adaptation rate given available variation, separates endangered from extinct (minimum viable population), and separates background from mass extinction.

checkQuestion: As the climate warms very fast, someone says: 'Don't worry — animals will just evolve quickly to cope with the heat, so they won't go extinct.' Is that reasoning sound? Explain when a species CAN adapt in time and when it can't.
checkAnswer: No. Adaptation by natural selection needs pre-existing heritable variation and many generations; a species can only keep up if the environment changes slower than that. When change is very fast — or the population is small with little variation, or slow to breed — it can't produce the adaptations in time and goes extinct. Evolution isn't an on-demand rescue; it can't be summoned just because it's needed.
